pos: n. (1572–1638; Patriarch of Constantinople, who issued a Reformed confession and was strangled by the Turks)
etymology: Lucaris, from the Greek surname Loukaris; Cyril, from Greek Kurillos, lordly, from kurios, lord.
biblical_def: Cyril Lucaris was a Cretan, educated at Venice and Padua, who was sent as a young man to Poland-Lithuania to resist the Union of Brest and there met the Reformed churches at first hand. He became Patriarch of Alexandria and then, in several troubled tenures between 1620 and 1638, Patriarch of Constantinople. He corresponded with Abbot and with the Dutch and Swiss churches, kept Geneva's chaplain Antoine Leger at his side, sent Greek students to Oxford, authorised a translation of the New Testament into spoken Greek, and in 1629 published at Geneva a Confession of the Eastern Church that was Reformed on Scripture, election, the two sacraments and images. He was deposed and restored five times by Ottoman politics, and in June 1638 was taken out by janissaries and strangled. The dictionary records him because he held a seat in a hostile place and kept his confession in it: “I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is” (Rev 2:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a patriarch as the chief bishop of certain ancient sees; a confession as a formulary comprising the articles of faith; and to please men as to court the favour of men rather than of God.
webster_full: PATRIARCH, n. [Gr. patriarches.] A dignitary superior to the order of archbishops; the chief bishop over several countries or provinces.
CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a belief; a formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised.
PLEASE, v.t. [L. placeo.] To excite agreeable sensations or emotions in; to gratify; to humor; to satisfy.
SUBJECTION, n. The act of subduing; the state of being under the power or control of another.
SEAT, n. That on which one sits; a chair; the place of sitting; a throne; residence of power.

I know thy works, and where thou dwellest, even where Satan's seat is: and thou holdest fast my name, and hast not denied my faith, even in those days wherein Antipas was my faithful martyr, who was slain among you, where Satan dwelleth.
Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
corruption_summary: Patriarch of Constantinople, who published a Reformed Confession of the Eastern Church at Geneva in 1629 and was strangled by janissaries in June 1638.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The genuine controversy is about Lucaris himself, and the dictionary states its reading rather than borrowing either side's. Orthodox writers since the Synod of Jerusalem have treated the 1629 confession as a forgery, or as the work of a man deceived by Western agents, or as a political manoeuvre against Rome. Reformed writers have sometimes claimed him as simply a Calvinist. Neither is satisfactory. The confession is his; the Reformed doctrine in it is real and was not extracted from him; and he also remained a Greek patriarch who never left his church and whose reform was meant to be of it and not out of it.

The principle to recover is that the truth of the gospel is not a thing a man may concede by degrees for the sake of his position. Paul will not yield an hour of it: “To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you” (Gal 2:5), and he puts the alternative as a straight question about whose approval a minister is working for — “for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal 1:10). The commendation to the church at Pergamos is for holding fast where Satan's seat is (Rev 2:13), and Hebrews lists what it has cost (Heb 11:37).

pos: n. (the Reformed confession of faith published at Geneva in 1629 by the Patriarch of Constantinople)
etymology: From Latin confessio, an acknowledgment; con, together, and fateri, to own or avow.
biblical_def: The Confessio fidei of Cyril Lucaris was printed in Latin at Geneva in 1629 and in Greek with additions in 1633. Its eighteen chapters are Reformed in substance: the Trinity and the person of Christ in the ancient terms; Scripture as the authority above the church rather than beneath it; predestination as God's eternal election in Christ and not a foreknowledge of merit; justification by faith; two sacraments and not seven, with the presence of Christ in the Supper received by faith; and a rejection of the veneration of images. Appended questions dealt with the canon, the invocation of saints and the reading of Scripture by the laity, which it defended. The confession was condemned at Constantinople in 1638, at Jassy in 1642 and at Jerusalem in 1672. The dictionary records it as a real confession of the Reformed faith from the Greek East, measured by the standard it set for itself: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to predestinate as to predetermine or foreordain; to elect as to choose, to select for favour; and testimony as the divine law, the whole divine revelation.
webster_full: PREDESTINATE, v.t. [L. praedestino.] To predetermine or foreordain; to appoint or ordain beforehand by an unchangeable purpose.
ELECT, v.t. [L. electus.] To choose; to select from among two or more; in theology, to designate, choose or select as an object of mercy.
TESTIMONY, n. A solemn declaration; in Scripture, the divine law, the two tables, the whole of divine revelation.
CANON, n. [Gr. kanon, a rule.] A law or rule; the genuine books of Scripture, called the sacred canon.
LIGHT, n. That which renders objects visible; illumination; figuratively, knowledge, truth, the gospel.

To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Eph 1:4
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
Gal 2:5
To whom we gave place by subjection, no, not for an hour; that the truth of the gospel might continue with you.
corruption_summary: The eighteen-chapter Reformed confession printed at Geneva in 1629, condemned at Constantinople in 1638, at Jassy in 1642 and at Jerusalem in 1672.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption attached to this document is the long effort to unwrite it. From 1638 onward it has been declared a Western forgery, a document Lucaris was tricked into signing, a private opinion with no standing, or a political instrument against Rome. The dictionary observes that the manuscript evidence, the Greek edition of 1633 with Lucaris's own expansions, and his twenty years of correspondence all tell against every one of those readings. A church may judge a confession wrong; it may not pretend the confession was never made.

The principle to recover is the test the confession itself applied, which is the only test by which it or any other may be judged. Isaiah states it as a rule of appeal: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). On that footing the confession's chapter on election stands or falls with Paul's chain — “Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified” (Rom 8:30) — and with the date he assigns to the choosing: “before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4). A confession is not a party badge; it is a claim about what the text says.

pos: n. (1589–1639; Lucaris's student, sent to Oxford, author of a Confession of the Eastern Church and Patriarch of Alexandria)
etymology: Kritopoulos, from Greek krites, a judge, with the patronymic poulos, son of; Metrophanes, from meter, mother, and phaino, to appear.
biblical_def: Metrophanes Kritopoulos was a monk of Mount Athos whom Lucaris sent to England in 1617 to study: he was at Balliol College, Oxford, for five years, then travelled through Germany and Switzerland meeting Lutheran and Reformed divines, and ended as Patriarch of Alexandria from 1636 until his death in 1639. At Helmstedt in 1625 he wrote, for the Lutherans who asked him, a Confession of the Eastern Church in twenty-three chapters. It is a more cautious and more thoroughly Orthodox document than Lucaris's: it holds to two sacraments proper with five lesser rites, denies transubstantiation but not a real presence, defends the veneration of icons as honour and not worship, and declines to adopt predestination. The dictionary records him because his method was the right one even where his conclusions differed: he went, read, examined and then wrote. “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to prove as to try, to ascertain by experiment or test; to contend as to strive earnestly in argument; and a cause as that which is pleaded, a suit or action.
webster_full: PROVE, v.t. [L. probo.] To try; to ascertain by an experiment or test; to evince, establish or ascertain as truth.
CONTEND, v.i. [L. contendo.] To strive in debate; to dispute earnestly; to strive for.
CAUSE, n. [L. causa.] A suit or action in court; that which a party pleads for; reason, motive.
TRY, v.t. To examine; to make experiment on; to prove by a test.
DILIGENCE, n. [L. diligentia.] Steady application in business; care; heed; constant effort.
scriptures: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world.
He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Lucaris's student, five years at Balliol College Oxford, author of the 1625 Confession of the Eastern Church, and Patriarch of Alexandria from 1636.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does exist partly to resist a temptation on the dictionary's own side. Kritopoulos is sometimes written up by Protestants as a disappointment: sent to Oxford at Reformed expense and came back insufficiently Reformed. That is a poor way to treat a man who did exactly what he was sent to do. He studied the Western churches at length and in person, formed his own judgment, wrote it down with his name on it, and disagreed in several places. A church that funds study and then resents the conclusions did not want study.

The principle to recover is that testing is commanded and that its outcome is not prescribed in advance: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21). John makes the same demand of the spirits and gives the reason — “because many false prophets are gone out into the world” (1Jn 4:1). Proverbs warns how convincing a case sounds when only one side has been heard: “He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him” (Pro 18:17). And the faith contended for is the one once delivered, not one newly constructed (Jud 1:3).

pos: n. (1549–1602; Greek scholar and Bishop of Cythera, who corresponded with the German divines about the procession of the Spirit)
etymology: Margunius, from the Greek surname Margounios; Maximus, from Latin maximus, greatest.
biblical_def: Maximus Margunius was a Cretan, educated at Padua, who lived mostly at Venice among the Greek community there, was made Bishop of Cythera in 1579 and never managed to take possession of the see because the Venetian authorities obstructed him. He was one of the finest Greek patristic scholars of his generation, edited texts, wrote hymns, and corresponded at length with German Lutherans, particularly with the Tubingen theologians and the Augsburg scholar David Hoeschel, on the question that divides the Greek and Latin churches: whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone or from the Father and the Son. He argued the Greek position with more learning and less heat than most, and was attacked by his own side for conceding too much to the Latins. The dictionary records him because the texts he argued from are the ones that settle the question: “even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me” (Joh 15:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines procession as the act of proceeding or issuing forth; a comforter as one who administers consolation, the Holy Spirit; and patristic as pertaining to the ancient fathers of the Christian church.
webster_full: PROCESSION, n. [L. processio.] The act of proceeding or issuing forth; in theology, the emanation of the Holy Spirit.
COMFORTER, n. One who administers comfort or consolation; the Holy Spirit, in Scripture called the Paraclete.
PATRISTIC, a. Pertaining to the ancient fathers of the Christian church, or to their writings.
PROCEED, v.i. [L. procedo.] To move, pass or go forward from one place to another; to issue or come forth as from a source.
TESTIFY, v.i. [L. testificor.] To make a solemn declaration to prove some fact; to bear witness.
scriptures: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, he shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you.
Act 2:33
Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear.
Rom 8:9
But ye are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you. Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.
corruption_summary: Greek patristic scholar and Bishop of Cythera, who corresponded with the Tubingen Lutherans on the procession of the Holy Spirit and was attacked by Greeks for conceding too much.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse of the filioque question is to make it either trivial or total. Some treat the clause as a thousand-year quarrel over a preposition that should be dropped for the sake of unity; others treat the Eastern position as a denial of Christ's deity, which it is not and never was. Margunius is useful precisely because he treated it as a genuine question of exegesis, argued it from the fathers and the text, and was willing to say where the Latins had a point. That is how a real disagreement is handled.

The principle to recover is that the Spirit's relation to Father and Son is stated in Scripture and not left to inference alone. The Lord says he will send the Comforter and that the Comforter proceeds from the Father: “even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me” (Joh 15:26). He also says the Father sends him in the Son's name (Joh 14:26), that the risen Christ received the promise of the Holy Ghost and shed it forth (Act 2:33), and that the Spirit is called the Spirit of Christ: “Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his” (Rom 8:9).

pos: n. (c. 1585–1646; Greek monk who set up the first printing press in Constantinople, and saw it destroyed)
etymology: Metaxas, from Greek metaxa, raw silk; Nicodemus, from Greek nike, victory, and demos, people.
biblical_def: Nicodemus Metaxas was a Cephalonian who went to London, learned the printing trade there, and in 1627 shipped a press and Greek type to Constantinople at Cyril Lucaris's invitation, setting it up in the grounds of the English embassy. It was the first printing press in the city. He printed works against the Jews and against the Latins and a treatise of Lucaris's, and in January 1628 the Jesuits persuaded the Ottoman authorities that the press was printing sedition. Janissaries raided it, broke the press and scattered the type, and Metaxas was expelled; he returned to the islands and was Archbishop of Cephalonia from 1629. Greek printing went back to Venice for another century and a half. The dictionary records him because the burning of a book is an old move with a recorded outcome: “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words” (Jer 36:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a press as a machine for printing; a penknife as a small knife for making or mending pens; and a roll as a volume, a writing formed into a cylinder.
webster_full: PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed; a machine for printing, called a printing press.
PENKNIFE, n. A small knife used for making and mending pens.
ROLL, n. A writing formed into a cylinder; a volume; a scroll; a register; a catalogue.
HEARTH, n. A pavement or floor of brick or stone in a chimney, on which a fire is made.
CONSUME, v.t. [L. consumo.] To destroy by separating the parts; to burn up; to waste; to spend.
scriptures: Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.

And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.
Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.
corruption_summary: Greek monk who learned printing in London and set up the first press in Constantinople in 1627; it was broken by janissaries in January 1628 at Jesuit instigation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary should say plainly who did what, since the episode is often reported vaguely. The press was broken by Ottoman soldiers, but the complaint that produced the raid came from the Jesuit mission in the city, which told the authorities that a Greek press under English protection was a political danger. A Christian order used a Muslim government's police power to destroy a Christian printing press. That is the fact, and naming it is not anti-Catholic polemic; it is the record.

The principle to recover is that destroying the copy does not destroy the word, and Scripture gives the case in detail. Jehoiakim cuts the scroll up and burns it column by column: “he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth” (Jer 36:23). The reply is immediate and unimpressed: “Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words” (Jer 36:28) — and the second edition is longer than the first, since “there were added besides unto them many like words” (Jer 36:32). The Lord fixes the durability of his own words above that of the world (Mat 24:35).

pos: n. (c. 1590–after 1631; Greek who studied at Wittenberg and printed a Greek catechism there in 1622)
etymology: Gerganos, from the Greek surname Gerganos; Zacharias, from Hebrew Zekaryah, the LORD hath remembered.
biblical_def: Zacharias Gerganos was a Greek from Arta who came to Wittenberg about 1619 and studied there for three years at the expense of Saxon patrons who hoped the Greek church might be won to the Reformation. In 1622 he published at Wittenberg a Christian Catechism in Greek, the first Greek catechism printed in the West by a Greek: it taught from the Scriptures, attacked the papacy sharply, criticised the invocation of saints and the veneration of images, and was circulated in the Greek lands. He went back and held church office in Greece, and the catechism was later condemned as Lutheranising. The dictionary records him because a catechism is a trained answer, and giving one is a duty laid on every Christian and not only on scholars: “and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a catechism as a form of instruction by question and answer; philosophy as the knowledge of natural causes and effects, hence vain speculation; and an imagination as a conception, a scheme formed in the mind.
webster_full: CATECHISM, n. A form of instruction by means of questions and answers, particularly in the principles of religion.
PHILOSOPHY, n. [Gr. philos, loving, and sophia, wisdom.] Literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of natural causes and effects; reasoning, speculation.
IMAGINATION, n. The power of the mind to form conceptions; a conceit, a scheme or notion formed in the mind.
RUDIMENT, n. [L. rudimentum.] A first principle or element; that which is to be first learnt.
TRADITION, n. [L. traditio.] The delivery of opinions, doctrines or customs from father to son, by oral communication.
scriptures: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
Col 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ;
Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
corruption_summary: Greek from Arta who studied at Wittenberg and printed the first Greek catechism in the West in 1622, afterwards condemned as Lutheranising.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a fair criticism of the Wittenberg project that produced Gerganos, and the dictionary makes it. German Protestants who funded Greek students in the hope of converting an ancient church did so with very little understanding of that church and a good deal of wishful thinking, and the pamphlets and catechisms that came out of it often read as German theology in Greek dress rather than as Greek theology reformed. Gerganos's catechism is better than most and still shows the marks.

The principle to recover is that every Christian is to be a catechised man with an answer ready, and that the answer is to be given with a particular manner: “and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear” (1Pe 3:15). Paul warns what fills the vacuum where catechesis is missing — “Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men” (Col 2:8) — and describes the work of bringing every thought under obedience to Christ (2Co 10:5). The measure throughout is the written word (Isa 8:20).

pos: n. (1570–1646; Lucaris's head of the Patriarchal Academy, an Aristotelian philosopher deposed after his patron's death)
etymology: Corydalleus, from the Attic district Korydallos; Theophilus, from Greek theos, God, and philos, loving.
biblical_def: Theophilus Corydalleus was an Athenian who studied at Rome and then at Padua under Cremonini, and taught philosophy at Venice, Zante and Athens before Cyril Lucaris brought him to Constantinople about 1625 to head the Patriarchal Academy. He reorganised it around Aristotle read in the Paduan manner, which is to say read as natural philosophy rather than as a servant of theology, and his commentaries were used in Greek schools for a century and a half. After Lucaris was strangled in 1638 Corydalleus was accused of Calvinism and of heterodoxy, deposed, and briefly imprisoned; he conformed, was made Metropolitan of Arta, and was deposed from that too. The dictionary records him with Paul's warning about knowledge held apart from charity: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an academy as a school or seminary of learning; craftiness as cunning, artifice, stratagem; and to puff up as to inflate with pride or vanity.
webster_full: ACADEMY, n. A school or seminary of learning; a society of learned men united for the promotion of arts and sciences.
CRAFTINESS, n. Cunning; artifice; stratagem; dexterity in devising and effecting what is contrary to truth.
PUFF, v.t. To swell with air; to inflate; to inflate with pride or vanity; to elate.
EDIFY, v.t. To instruct and improve the mind in knowledge, particularly in moral and religious knowledge.
PRUDENT, a. Cautious; circumspect; practically wise; discreet.
scriptures: Now as touching things offered unto idols, we know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth.
And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and will bring to nothing the understanding of the prudent.
corruption_summary: Head of the Patriarchal Academy at Constantinople under Lucaris, who taught Aristotle in the Paduan manner; deposed after 1638 on charges of Calvinism and heterodoxy.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a real argument in Corydalleus's case worth stating from both ends. His defenders hold that he brought the Greek schools into contact with serious philosophy at a moment when Greek learning under Ottoman rule was in danger of dying entirely, and that is true. His accusers held that reading Aristotle as the Paduans did — as an autonomous natural philosophy with its own conclusions, not answerable to revelation — was the beginning of a method that would end by making theology one subject among others. That also turned out to be true.

The principle to recover is that knowledge is never neutral about the man who holds it. Paul grants the knowledge and then sets the two effects against each other: “Knowledge puffeth up, but charity edifieth” (1Co 8:1), and he undercuts the confidence directly — “And if any man think that he knoweth any thing, he knoweth nothing yet as he ought to know” (1Co 8:2). The verdict of the world's wisdom before God is stated without qualification: “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1Co 3:19), and God's own announced intention concerning it is destruction (1Co 1:19).

pos: n. (d. c. 1633; translator of the New Testament into spoken Greek, printed at Geneva in 1638)
etymology: Maximos, from Latin maximus, greatest; Gallipoli, from Greek Kallipolis, the beautiful city.
biblical_def: Maximos Kallipolites was a monk of Gallipoli whom Cyril Lucaris commissioned to translate the New Testament out of the Greek of the original into the spoken Greek of his own day, on the ground that ordinary Greeks could no longer understand the text read in their churches. He worked at it with Antoine Leger, Geneva's chaplain at Constantinople, finished it about 1632, and died before it was printed. It came off the press at Geneva in 1638, with the original and the vernacular in parallel columns and a preface defending the whole enterprise, in the same year Lucaris was strangled. It was attacked at once as a Protestant intrusion and the later synods condemned it. The dictionary records him because the Lord's own parable makes understanding the difference between the seed that is snatched away and the seed that bears: “and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart” (Mat 13:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vernacular as native, belonging to the country of one's birth; plain as evident, clear, not obscure; and to enlighten as to make clear to the understanding, to instruct.
webster_full: VERNACULAR, a. [L. vernaculus.] Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
PLAIN, a. Evident to the understanding; clear; manifest; not obscure or difficult.
ENLIGHTEN, v.t. To make clear to the understanding; to instruct; to illuminate with knowledge.
HUNDREDFOLD, n. A hundred times as much; the increase of a hundred to one.
STATUTE, n. [L. statutum.] An act of the legislature; a law; a special law or decree.
scriptures: When any one heareth the word of the kingdom, and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown in his heart. This is he which received seed by the way side.
But he that received seed into the good ground is he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit, and bringeth forth, some an hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.
Pro 8:9
They are all plain to him that understandeth, and right to them that find knowledge.
Psa 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
corruption_summary: Monk of Gallipoli commissioned by Cyril Lucaris to translate the New Testament into spoken Greek; completed about 1632 and printed at Geneva in 1638, the year Lucaris died.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is the argument used against the translation, which is the oldest argument there is and is still in use. It was said that the received Greek text was sacred in its form as well as its substance, that a vernacular rendering would flatten its mysteries, and that the people did not need to understand what they heard so much as to receive it reverently. The dictionary answers that an unintelligible reading is not a reverent one, and notes that the same arguments were made in Latin against the same work in the West, by men who would not have accepted them about any other book.

The principle to recover is that understanding is not an optional refinement of hearing but the thing that distinguishes fruitful hearing from the other kind. The Lord's own exposition of the sower turns on it: the wayside hearer is the one of whom it is said “and understandeth it not, then cometh the wicked one” (Mat 13:19). The good ground is described by the same faculty working: “he that heareth the word, and understandeth it; which also beareth fruit” (Mat 13:23). Wisdom claims to be plain to the man who will understand (Pro 8:9), and the Psalm says what the commandment does when it is received: “the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes” (Psa 19:8).

pos: n. (the Moldavian council of 1642 which condemned Lucaris's confession and adopted Mogila's in its place)
etymology: Jassy, the German and Latin form of Romanian Iasi, the Moldavian capital; of disputed derivation.
biblical_def: The Synod of Jassy met in the Moldavian capital in 1642 under the patronage of the prince Vasile Lupu, with Greek and Ruthenian clergy present, and was called to deal with the Confession of Cyril Lucaris. It condemned the confession and its Reformed articles point by point, examined and amended the Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila, the Metropolitan of Kiev, and commended that as the Eastern church's answer. Mogila's confession is framed against the Reformed positions throughout: it teaches seven sacraments, transubstantiation in substance if not in Latin terminology, the veneration of icons, and the authority of tradition alongside Scripture. The dictionary records the synod as a real council doing real business, and sets beside it the standard by which any council's decrees must be weighed: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a synod as an ecclesiastical council; to diminish as to lessen, to take away a part; and accursed as doomed to destruction, separated.
webster_full: SYNOD, n. [Gr. sunodos, a coming together.] A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.
DIMINISH, v.t. [L. diminuo.] To lessen; to make less or smaller by any means; to take away a part.
ACCURSED, participle passive. Doomed to destruction or misery; separated; devoted to destruction.
DECREE, n. [L. decretum.] Judicial decision; an edict or law made by a council or superior authority.
FIGURE, n. [L. figura.] The form of any thing; a representation; a mode of speech in which a word is used otherwise than literally.
scriptures: Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Gal 1:9
As we said before, so say I now again, If any man preach any other gospel unto you than that ye have received, let him be accursed.

And these things, brethren, I have in a figure transferred to myself and to Apollos for your sakes; that ye might learn in us not to think of men above that which is written, that no one of you be puffed up for one against another.
corruption_summary: The Moldavian council of 1642 which condemned the Confession of Cyril Lucaris and commended Peter Mogila's Orthodox Confession in its place.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two uses of this synod should be refused. The dictionary will not pretend it was a sham: it was a genuine council of Eastern bishops, it read the documents, and it decided against the Reformed articles for reasons it stated. Neither will it accept the claim sometimes built on it that the Eastern church had thereby shown that Lucaris never meant what he wrote. A council may condemn a confession; the condemnation does not retroactively unmake the confession, and Jassy's own proceedings assume Lucaris wrote it.

The principle to recover is that every council, East or West, stands under a word it did not write and may neither extend nor trim. Moses states the rule in both directions: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2). Paul puts an anathema on any other gospel and includes himself and an angel in the scope of it: “But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). He then repeats it, in case anyone took the first for rhetoric: “As we said before, so say I now again” (Gal 1:9). And he teaches the Corinthians “not to think of men above that which is written” (1Co 4:6).

pos: n. (1641–1707; Patriarch of Jerusalem, who convened the Synod of Jerusalem in 1672 against Reformed doctrine)
etymology: Dositheus, from Greek dosis, a gift, and theos, God; a name meaning God-given.
biblical_def: Dositheus II Notaras became Patriarch of Jerusalem in 1669 at twenty-eight and held the see for thirty-eight years, a formidable administrator, controversialist and collector of manuscripts. In 1672 he convened at Bethlehem the Synod of Jerusalem, which issued a confession in his name answering the Reformed articles directly: six chapters affirming the authority of tradition with Scripture, seven mysteries, transubstantiation, the veneration of icons and the saints, prayers for the dead, and free will against predestination; and it repudiated the Confession of Cyril Lucaris as not the faith of the Eastern church. He also printed a great deal of polemic against both Rome and the Reformed. The dictionary records him as the East's clearest and most honest answer to the Reformation, and sets the Lord's own test against its central claim: “Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered” (Mar 7:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tradition as the delivery of doctrines or customs from father to son by oral communication; a mystery as something hidden which God has revealed, a sacrament; and to frustrate as to defeat, to render of no effect.
webster_full: TRADITION, n. [L. traditio.] The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity.
MYSTERY, n. [Gr. musterion.] A profound secret; something hidden which God has revealed; among the Greeks, a sacrament.
FRUSTRATE, v.t. [L. frustror.] To defeat; to disappoint; to balk; to render of no effect.
PLAGUE, n. [L. plaga, a stroke.] Any thing troublesome or vexatious; a pestilence; a divine judgment.
REPROVE, v.t. To blame; to censure; to charge with a fault to the face.
scriptures: Mar 7:13
Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.
Mar 7:9
And he said unto them, Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition.
Pro 30:6
Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
corruption_summary: Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1669, who convened the 1672 Synod of Jerusalem and issued a confession affirming tradition, seven mysteries and free will against the Reformed articles.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The dictionary should say what it respects here before it says where it disagrees. Dositheus did not evade: he read the Reformed confessions, stated the Eastern position article by article against them, signed it, and published it. That is more creditable than the common course of declaring an opponent's confession a forgery, which his predecessors at Jassy had edged toward. Where the dictionary dissents is on the premise, and the dissent is total: a tradition set alongside Scripture as a second source does not supplement the word but governs it, and whatever governs the word has displaced it.

The principle to recover is the Lord's own handling of exactly this claim, made by men who were not inventing their tradition and could trace it. He does not deny that they had received it; he denies what it had done: “Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered” (Mar 7:13), and he puts the mechanism in a sentence of flat irony — “Full well ye reject the commandment of God, that ye may keep your own tradition” (Mar 7:9). Proverbs forbids the addition and names its result: “Add thou not unto his words, lest he reprove thee, and thou be found a liar” (Pro 30:6).
